reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / Novak's Gynecology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Lactational mastitis is an inflammatory, usually infective, condition of the breast in a breastfeeding woman, presenting with a tender, hot, erythematous, wedge-shaped area often accompanied by fever and flu-like malaise
It typically begins with milk stasis from ineffective or infrequent drainage, which then becomes secondarily infected, most often by Staphylococcus aureus entering through a cracked or damaged nipple
Continued effective milk removal is the cornerstone of treatment; breastfeeding from the affected side should continue and is safe for the infant
Supportive measures include frequent feeding or expression, correcting attachment and positioning, warmth before feeds and cold after for comfort, adequate hydration, rest, and simple analgesia

Antibiotics active against Staphylococcus aureus are indicated when symptoms are severe, systemic, or fail to improve within a short period of conservative management, or when a nipple fissure is infected
A localised fluctuant, non-resolving mass suggests a breast abscess, which requires drainage by needle aspiration or incision alongside antibiotics
Failure to improve with appropriate treatment should prompt consideration of an abscess or, in a non-lactating or persistent case, inflammatory breast cancer
Prevention centres on good breastfeeding technique, ensuring full drainage, avoiding abrupt weaning, and prompt attention to nipple trauma
Recurrent mastitis warrants review of feeding technique and evaluation for a persistent focus or underlying breast pathology
reference.pathophysiology: Inadequate or infrequent milk drainage leads to milk stasis and rising intraductal pressure, causing milk to leak into the surrounding stroma and provoke a local inflammatory response. Nipple trauma, commonly from poor latch, provides a portal of entry for skin flora, predominantly Staphylococcus aureus, so the stagnant milk becomes a culture medium and infection is established. If untreated, the localised infection can organise into a walled-off collection of pus, forming a breast abscess. The wedge-shaped distribution reflects involvement of a segment of the ductal-lobular system.
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory breast carcinoma (especially if non-lactating or non-resolving)
Candidal nipple or ductal infection causing pain
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis is usually sufficient; investigations are reserved for atypical or non-resolving cases
Breast milk culture and sensitivity where infection is severe, recurrent, hospital-associated, or unresponsive to first-line antibiotics
Breast ultrasound to identify or exclude an abscess when a fluctuant or non-resolving mass is present
Needle aspiration of a suspected abscess for both diagnosis and drainage with culture of the aspirate
Consideration of biopsy and specialist referral if inflammatory changes fail to resolve, to exclude malignancy
redFlags: A fluctuant or non-resolving mass indicating breast abscess requiring drainage
Systemic sepsis with high fever, rigors, tachycardia, or hypotension
Failure to respond to appropriate antibiotics and milk drainage within a few days
Persistent inflammatory changes, skin thickening, or peau d'orange raising concern for inflammatory breast cancer
Overlying skin breakdown or rapidly spreading erythema
reference.prognosis: Most cases resolve quickly with effective milk removal and, when needed, appropriate antibiotics, and breastfeeding can continue throughout. Delayed or inadequate treatment increases the risk of abscess formation, which then requires drainage. Recurrence is uncommon when feeding technique is optimised, and the majority of women recover fully without lasting effect on lactation.
pitfalls: Advising cessation of breastfeeding, which worsens stasis and prolongs the illness
Failing to recognise and drain a breast abscess, treating with antibiotics alone
Overlooking inflammatory breast cancer in non-lactating or persistent presentations
Not addressing the underlying poor attachment or drainage, leading to recurrence
Delaying antibiotics when systemic or severe features are present
management: Prioritise effective milk removal - continue breastfeeding from the affected breast, feed or express frequently, and correct attachment and positioning
Add supportive measures: warmth before feeds, cold compresses afterwards, simple analgesia such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, rest and adequate hydration

Prescribe antibiotics active against Staphylococcus aureus, such as flucloxacillin or a macrolide or clindamycin if penicillin-allergic, when symptoms are severe, systemic, associated with an infected fissure or failing to improve with conservative care
Investigate a fluctuant or non-resolving mass with ultrasound and drain a confirmed abscess by needle aspiration or incision, sending pus for culture
Send breast-milk culture in severe, recurrent, hospital-associated or unresponsive infection to guide antibiotic choice
Provide lactation-consultant support and refer for biopsy to exclude inflammatory carcinoma if inflammation does not resolve
Safety-net with clear advice to return if symptoms worsen or a collection develops
